           COMES NOW Staff of the Missouri Public Service Commission (“Staff”), by and

through undersigned counsel, and for its Post-Hearing Brief states as follows:

                                              INTRODUCTION

           In this general rate case, the Commission must exercise its delegated authority to set

prospective rates for Evergy Missouri Metro, Inc., d/b/a Every Missouri Metro (“EMM”) a task

that involves balancing the interests of ratepayers, the utility, and a myriad of other

intervening parties with disparate interests and differing ideas about the issues and policies

presented. The Commission must weigh the evidence presented before it to come to its

ultimate goal in setting rates that are “just and reasonable,” which is a rate that provides

sufficient revenue to cover EMM’s costs in providing electric service, allows EMM

shareholders a reasonable opportunity to earn a fair return on their investment, but is no

more than necessary to meet those goals, which protects the rate-paying residents and

businesses EMM serves.1

                                           LEGAL STANDARD

        Each proceeding for fixing of rates of a public utility company must be determined

upon its own facts. The rate of return for a public utility is determined by a calculation that

factors in: (1) the ratio of debt and equity to total capital; and (2) the cost and (3) weighted

cost for each of these capital components. 3

        The Commission has authority under Chapters 386 and 393, RSMo, to regulate public

utility rates and to ensure rates are “just and reasonable” 4 after considering all relevant

factors.5 EMM is a public utility, and an electric corporation, as those terms are defined in

Section 386.020(15) and (43), RSMo. As such, EMM is subject to the jurisdiction of the

Commission pursuant to Chapters 386 and 393, RSMo.

        The United States Supreme Court in the Hope case established that the rate making

process involves a balancing of the investor and consumer interests. 6 It also established in

         The Commission sets just and reasonable rates via a two-step process using

traditional cost-of-service ratemaking. 15 First, the “revenue requirement” must be

determined, that is, the amount of income the utility needs on an annual basis. 16 This is

determined by matching expenses, investments, and revenue, 17 and the relationship

between the three is the fundamental building block of Missouri ratemaking. 18

This relationship is examined during the test year, and the Missouri Court of Appeals

described the test year as follows:

                    The test year is the primary mechanism through which the PSC
             determines appropriate rates. The PSC focuses on four factors during
             the test year: (1) the rate of return the utility has an opportunity to earn;
             (2) the rate base upon which a return may be earned; (3) the
             depreciation costs of plant and equipment; and (4) allowable operating
             expenses. These factors are considered to determine the utility's
             revenue requirement, which is the amount of revenue taxpayers must
             generate to pay the costs of producing the utility's services they receive
             while yielding a reasonable rate of return. The PSC's use of a true-up
             audit and hearing is designed to balance the historical data with known
             and measurable subsequent and future changes; these are generally
             limited only to accounts affected by a significant known and
             measurable change, such as a new labor contract, new tax rate, or the
             completion of a new capital asset. This procedure is designed to
             reduce regulatory lag.19

         Second, after the revenue requirement is determined, rates must be designed in a

manner that, given the usage characteristics of the utility’s customers, will produce the

necessary revenue, with no class significantly under- or over-contributing to the overall

revenue produced.20 Fair rates match costs and cost causers, so that similarly situated

customers pay the same rates. Appropriate rate design is shaped in the context of a class

cost of service study. From there, interclass revenue responsibility shifts, as applicable,

are designed to bring each class closer to producing the system-average rate of return used

in determining the recommended revenue requirement. A well-designed CCOS 21 will

produce rates that are non-discriminatory and based upon principles of cost causation.

That is not to say that that rates or rate increases must be the same for each class, as

“discrimination as to rates is not unlawful where based upon a reasonable classification

corresponding to actual differences in the situation of the consumers or the furnishing of the

service.”22

        Additionally, rate design may include considerations beyond recovering the

necessary revenue requirement. These objectives may be fairness, simplicity, stability,

avoidance of undue discrimination or preferences, efficiency, and conservation. 23

Avoidance of rate shock and affordability concerns are also top-of-mind across the industry.

Issue 25: Fuel Adjustment Clause – Large Load Power Service

               History and Operation of Missouri Fuel Adjustment Clause

       The Fuel Adjustment Clause (“FAC”) allows an electric utility to adjust what it charges

customers for certain electricity-supply costs without having to ﬁle a new general rate case

every time those costs change. It is authorized under § 386.266.1, RSMo., and implemented

through Commission Rule 20 CSR 4240-20.090.

       For EMM, these costs include more than the fuel burned at power plants. They also

include certain costs of purchasing electricity, associated wholesale-market transactions,

and revenues from selling electricity.

       The underlying idea is that electricity-supply costs ﬂuctuate much more frequently

than the rates approved in a traditional rate case. For example, EMM operates a variety

                                               77
 of generation assets which burn coal, use nuclear fuel, or use natural gas.            EMM

also participates in a regional wholesale electricity market operated by the Southwest

Power Pool (“SPP”).

       The costs and revenues discussed above together are referred to as Net Base Energy

Costs (“NBEC”). In a general rate case, these costs and revenues are estimated, based on a

normalized or annualized level as of the update period and revised again at true-up. The base

factor is calculated as the NBEC divided by the Net System Input (“NSI”). NSI is an estimate

of the normalized amount of electricity required to meet the energy demands of both the

company's customers and its own needs at the generation level. During a rate case, with

proper information, the relationship of the FAC base factor and permanent rates can be

aligned. The base factor then gets used in the subsequent Fuel Adjustment Rate (“FAR”)

ﬁlings, and it calculates the di erence between the actual net energy costs (“ANEC”)

and the NBEC.

       For example, assume the Commission approves electric rates assuming it will cost

EMM $100 million annually, net of certain revenues, to produce and purchase electricity.

The $100 million dollars would be considered the NBEC and is based upon the NSI included

in the determination of fuel and purchased power expense during the test period used

to determine the revenue requirement. Following the Commission’s order, coal prices

increase, natural gas becomes more expensive, and wholesale electricity prices change,

resulting in EMM’s actual net energy costs being $150 million. Without an FAC, EMM would

have to absorb that additional $50 million expense until it could seek recovery through

another permissible ratemaking process. With an FAC, EMM can recover an authorized


                                             78
 portion of the di erence between the net base energy costs and the actual net energy costs

through a separate charge on customers’ bills. A key point to highlight: the process works in

both directions. If actual net energy costs are lower than the amount reﬂected in base rates,

customers receive the applicable portion of the beneﬁt through a lower FAC charge.

       A common misunderstanding of the FAC is that it is the only way a utility like EMM

recovers all of its fuel costs; this is not accurate. Customers already pay for an expected

level of fuel and purchases power costs through their regular electricity rates based upon

the energy consumption reﬂected in the calculation of net fuel and purchased power

expense in the revenue requirement. The FAC generally adjusts for the di erence between

that expected level and actual eligible net energy costs.

       In a general rate case like this one, the Commission sets new base rates and

establishes the level of eligible net energy costs to be reﬂected in those rates; in essence,

the Commission is rebasing those costs. The new base rates will incorporate those eligible

net energy costs, and future FAC adjustments will measure eligible di erences

relative to the newly approved base factor and the actual net energy costs. The base

factor only represents the fuel and purchased power expense of the energy consumed during

the test period in the rate case.

        Net marginal rates are used in connection with the Missouri Energy Efficiency

Investment Act (“MEEIA”) to determine the contribution to utility margins associated with

customers’ electricity consumption. Because energy efficiency programs reduce electricity

consumption, the applicable net marginal rate is relevant to determining the margins

associated with those reductions. Accordingly, the calculation should reflect the rates

customers will actually pay, rather than rates that may change during the course of a general

rate proceeding.

        EMM witness Graham Jaynes provided net marginal rate calculations in

Schedule GAJ-12 to his direct testimony. Those calculations were based on EMM’s

Medium General Service, Large General Service, and Large Power Service classes. 446

However, Jaynes acknowledged that net marginal rates have traditionally been

updated at the conclusion of a rate case, after final rates have been determined. 447

Thus, while Schedule GAJ-12 provides the basis for the calculation, its results are

necessarily preliminary.
